      Abstract
The Max-DICUT problem has emerged as a canonical problem for understanding the approximability
of constraint satisfaction problems in the streaming model. A seminal result of Kapralov and Krachun
[STOC 2019] shows that it is impossible to beat 1/2-approximation for Max-DICUT in sublinear
space in the single-pass streaming setting, even on bounded-degree graphs. In a recent work, Saxena,
Singer, Sudan, and Velusamy [SODA 2025] prove that the above lower bound is tight by giving a
single-pass algorithm for bounded-degree graphs that achieves (1/2 − ϵ)-approximation in sublinear
space, for every constant ϵ > 0. For arbitrary graphs of unbounded degree, they give an O(1/ϵ)-pass
O(log n) space algorithm. Their work left open the question of obtaining 1/2-approximation for
arbitrary graphs in the single-pass setting in sublinear space. We make progress towards this question
and give a two-pass algorithm that achieves (1/2 − ϵ)-approximation in sublinear space, for every
constant ϵ > 0.

 1      Introduction

The maximum directed cut problem (Max-DICUT) is the analogue of the maximum cut
(Max-CUT) problem for directed graphs. In particular, given a directed graph G(V, E), the
Max-DICUT problem asks to find an ordered bipartition (a “left” set L and a “right” set R)
of the vertex set V that maximizes the number of edges that go from L to R. In contrast, in
Max-CUT, we measure all the edges that cross L and R. Both Max-CUT and Max-DICUT
are NP Hard and so, we study algorithms that approximately solve these problems. An
α-approximation algorithm is one that outputs a solution that has a value which is at least α
fraction of the optimum. Besides being fundamental problems in their own right, Max-CUT
and Max-DICUT also belong to a large class of combinatorial optimization problems called
the constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) which capture several fundamental optimization
problems in computer science. CSPs are well studied in theoretical computer science, owing in

          In many computational settings, Max-CUT has successfully served as a canonical prob-
      lem in the study of CSPs. For example, in the polynomial time setting, Goemans and
      Williamson [14] gave the first SDP-based approximation algorithm for Max-CUT. And on
      the lower bound side, conditioned on the Unique Games conjecture, Khot, Kindler, Mossell,
      and O’Donnell [20] constructed tight integrality gap instances showing that the Goemans-
      Williamson SDP for Max-CUT is optimal. In a breakthrough follow-up work, Raghavendra [22]
      generalized both these works to all CSPs and gives an optimal SDP-based characterization
      for the approximability of every CSP in polynomial time. However, in the streaming setting,
      Max-CUT does not capture all CSPs.
          In the single-pass streaming model of computation, the constraints of a CSP instance (or
      edges of a graph in the case of Max-CUT, Max-DICUT) arrive in a stream. The streaming
      algorithm is allowed one pass over this stream and is required to compute an approximation
      to the optimum value of the instance, using limited space. The amount of space available
      to the algorithm is typically parameterized by n, the number of variables in the instance
      (or vertices of the input graph in the case of Max-CUT, Max-DICUT). For every CSP, there
      exists a trivial sampling-based algorithm [1, 28] that can achieve (1 − ϵ)-approximation using
      Õ(n) space. Therefore, the interesting regime is when the algorithm is allowed only o(n)
      space. Surprisingly, Max-CUT has no non-trivial approximation in this regime! In particular,
      1/2-approximation is trivial (just output 1/2 for every input graph) since any graph has a
      bipartition with at least half the edges crossing the bipartition. A series of works [17, 18, 19],
      culminating with the breakthrough result of Kapralov and Krachun [19] show that for any
      constant ϵ > 0, any single-pass streaming algorithm that achieves (1/2 + ϵ)-approximation for
      Max-CUT requires Ω(n) space. A follow-up work due to Chou, Golovnev, Sudan, Velingker,
      and Velusamy [7] proves optimal inapproximability results for multiple CSPs in o(n) space,
      generalizing techniques from the Max-CUT lower bound [19].

    In the multi-pass setting, a streaming algorithm is allowed to do multiple passes over
the same stream of constraints. Assadi and Nagargoje [3] show that any p-pass algorithm
for Max-CUT achieving (1 − ϵ)-approximation requires at least Ω(n1−O(ϵp) ) space. A recent
breakthrough result of Fei, Minzer, and Wang [11] shows that for any ϵ > 0, any p-pass
algorithm for Max-CUT (also Max-DICUT) achieving (1/2 + ϵ)-approximation requires at
least Ω(n1/3 /p) space. In contrast, for dense instances of average degree at least nδ , a two-
pass streaming algorithm due to Bhaskara, Daruki, and Venkatasubramanian [5], achieves
(1 − ϵ)-approximation for Max-CUT (also Max-DICUT) using Õ(n1−δ ) space. An algorithm
due to Saxena, Singer, Sudan, and Velusamy achieves (1/2 − ϵ)-approximation on arbitrary
graphs in O(1/ϵ) passes using O(log n) space [25]. In a prior work [23], the same authors
give a two-pass algorithm that achieves 0.485-approximation using O(log n) space. A recent
result due to Fei, Minzer, and Wang [12] gives a dichotomy characterization in the multi-pass
setting based on the basic LP relaxation for every CSP. In particular, they show that the
techniques from [27, 25] can be combined with the distributed algorithms of Yoshida [29] to
obtain a streaming algorithm that solves the LP relaxation for every CSP in O(1/ϵ2 ) passes
and O(log n) space. And to beat the approximation achieved by the basic LP, any p-pass
streaming algorithm requires at least Ω(n1/3 /p) space.
    The connection between streaming algorithms and LP relaxations was also identified in a
concurrent work by Singer, Tulsiani, and Velusamy [26]. They conjecture that for every CSP,
there must be a single-pass o(n) space streaming algorithm that solves its LP relaxation,
and any algorithm beating this factor must require at least Ω(n) space. For Max-DICUT, its
basic LP achieves 1/2-approximation and so their conjecture states that there is a single-pass
algorithm that achieves 1/2-approximation in o(n) space. In this work, we make progress
towards this conjecture and prove it in the two-pass setting.

▶ Theorem 1.1 (Main result). For every ϵ > 0, there is a two-pass streaming algorithm
that achieves (1/2 − ϵ)-approximation for Max-DICUT on any n-vertex graph using space

 2     Technical overview

In this section, we present a technical overview of the proof of our main result.
    There are three main ingredients to our proof: 1) a single-pass (1/2 − ϵ)-approximation
algorithm of Saxena, Singer, Sudan, and Velusamy [25] for bounded-degree graphs that uses
O(n1−Ω(1) ) space, 2) Trevisan’s reduction [27] from unbounded-degree to bounded-degree
graphs that approximately preserves the Max-DICUT value, and 3) Bhaskara, Daruki, and
Venkatasubramanian’s [5] two-pass algorithm that achieves (1 − ϵ)-approximation on graphs
of average degree at least nδ using Õ(n1−δ ) space. The following theorems formally state
their results.

▶ Theorem 2.1 ([25]). For every d ∈ N and ϵ > 0, there is a single-pass streaming algorithm
that achieves (1/2 − ϵ)-approximation for Max-DICUT on any n-vertex graph of maximum
degree at most d using space O(n1−Ω(1) ).

▶ Theorem 2.2 ([27]). For any directed graph G(V, E) on n vertices and m edges, and 0 <
ϵ ≤ 1, there exists a (random) directed graph G(V , E) on 2m vertices and O(m/ϵ2 ) edges such
that with probability at least 5/6, Max-DICUT(G)−ϵ′ ≤ Max-DICUT(G) ≤ Max-DICUT(G)+ϵ,
and the maximum degree of a vertex in G is at most O(1/ϵ2 ).

          At a high level, our idea is to reduce the input graph which could potentially have an
      unbounded maximum degree to a bounded-degree graph using Trevisan’s reduction [27], and
      then execute the [25] algorithm for bounded-degree graphs. However, there are challenges to
      this naive approach. Firstly, Trevisan’s reduction is not a small-space reduction and requires
      the knowledge of the degree of every vertex in the graph. This would be too expensive to
      store in the streaming setting. Secondly, the reduction produces a graph with 2m vertices,
      which could be Θ(n2 ) in the worst case, hence the [25] algorithm could require Ω(n) space.
      We deal with the second challenge by running the [25] algorithm only when the input graph
      is sufficiently sparse, i.e., has at most n1+δ edges, for some suitably chosen δ so that the
      space usage is still at most O(n1−Ω(1) ). And when the input instance is dense, we run the [5]

      challenge, we implement the [25] algorithm in a non black-box manner. We do not produce
      the entire bounded-degree graph from the Trevisan reduction and instead only sample parts
      of this graph that are required for the [25] algorithm. Below, we give a high-level overview of

Putting them together (a three-pass algorithm). Since the [25] algorithm only requires the
induced subgraph of a randomly sampled subset of the vertex set, we do not need to do the
Trevisan reduction on the entire input graph. Instead, we directly sample a random subset
of vertices from the bounded-degree graph, i.e., from V ′ = {(v, i) : v ∈ V ; i ∈ [deg(v)]}, and
perform a partial Trevisan reduction on their parent vertices. To sample from V ′ , we first
map every edge e ∈ E, based on its position in the stream, to two unique vertices in V ′ , i.e.,
no two edges map to the same vertex. In particular, an edge u → v is mapped to (u, i) and
(v, j) iff it is the i-th edge (resp. j-th edge) incident on u (resp. v) in the stream. Thus, as the
edges arrive in the stream, we can sample from V ′ .4 Once the vertices are sampled, we have
to sample the induced subgraph on these vertices. The original Trevisan reduction performs a
global sampling of the edges, where every edge is sampled with probability proportional to its
weight. In order to perform such a sampling, one would have to compute the weights on all
the edges, which is infeasible in the streaming setting. We therefore modify the reduction to
a local sampling procedure, where for every edge u → v ∈ E, we create d = O(1/ϵ2 ) “copies”
of it in E ′ and for every copy of the edge, we independently sample a uniform random copy
of u and a uniform random copy of v in V ′ as its endpoints.5 We also delete all the edges
incident on high-degree vertices and not just the minimal set of edges, as it is not clear how
to compute the minimal set without generating the entire graph. We argue in Section 4
that this procedure still preserves the Max-DICUT value up to an additive ϵ factor with high
probability. Now that we have this local procedure, we generate the induced subgraph on
the sampled vertices as follows. After we sample the vertices in the first pass, we store the
degrees of their parent vertices in the second pass. In the third pass, we again scan through
the edges in the stream and if u → v is such that both u and v have at least one of their
copies sampled, then we sample d independent copies of the edge as outlined above (we can
do this since we know the degrees of u and v), and we store those edges that are in the
induced subgraph. If neither u nor v have any copies in the sampled set of vertices, then
we do nothing. If only one of them, say u, has sampled copies, then we sample only the
endpoints corresponding to u’s copies for the d copies of the edge. We do this to keep track
of the degrees of all the sampled vertices, and in the end, delete all the edges incident on the
high-degree vertices. The formal description of the procedure and the proof of correctness
are described in Section 5.

3.1    Neighborhood distributions and the simulation of local algorithms
A key contribution of Saxena, Singer, Sudan, and Velusamy in [25] is the identification of
a connection between streaming and local algorithms, where they show that it is possible
to estimate local neighborhood distributions of graphs in the streaming setting and use
these distributions to simulate constant-round distributed algorithms. We recall some of
the notations introduced in their paper and reprove their main theorem that shows that
sampling vertices uniformly at random and estimating local neighborhood distributions from
the induced subgraph suffices to estimate the value of a local algorithm that is executed on
the original graph.
   First, we formally define the LOCAL model for distributed algorithms for the Max-DICUT
problem and state the result of [6, 25].

▶ Definition 3.4 (The LOCAL model for distributed algorithms for Max-DICUT). Let G(V, E)
be a directed graph on n vertices and m edges. G describes the topology of a communication
network, where each node can communicate with both its incoming and outgoing neighbors.
Communication happens in synchronous rounds, where in every round, every node does some
internal computations and sends an arbitrarily long message to each of its neighbors. At
the end, each node v computes a fractional assignment ρ(v) ∈ [0, 1] and the approximation
ratio achieved by the algorithm is defined to be DICUT(G, ρ)/Max-DICUT(G). In randomized
algorithms, the nodes also have access to an arbitrarily long private random bit string that is
sampled prior to any communication between the nodes.
